notes.short: Job's friends as the only wise men: said in irony
notes.about: Job seems to grant that his friends are the only wise people, so that wisdom will die with them. He means the opposite, as the next verse says: “I am not inferior to you.” Their speeches had told him nothing he did not know.

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die
figure.means: that his friends were no wiser than he was, for all their claim to teach him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under irony spoken by men: Job's friends had no more knowledge than he. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the words are meant as irony, as if all understanding were theirs alone. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls them ironical, Clarke a strong irony, and Henry says Job speaks ironically of their claim to all wisdom.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: This powerful Irony is meant to emphasise the fact that Job’s friends had no more knowledge than he

cites.quote: is intended as irony: ye are not merely single individuals, but the people = race of men ... so that all human understanding is confined to you, and there is none other to be found; and when once you die, it will seem to have died out.

cites.quote: Ironical, as if all the wisdom in the world was concentrated in them and would expire when they expired.

notes.short: Night, then morning; then back to the night
notes.about: Verse 19 can be read as the wicked man's sudden end, either in the night after he lies down, or by day after he opens his eyes. Verse 20 then answers the two crosswise: first terrors like a flood, then a tempest in the night, so the night opens and closes the picture.

lines.words: He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more;
when he opens his eyes, all is gone.
Terrors overtake him like a flood;
a tempest sweeps him away in the night.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) reads verse 19 as sudden death, either in the night after the man lies down rich or by day after he opens his eyes in the morning, and says the two lines of verse 20 are attached crosswise to that picture of destruction by night or by day: the terrors of death seize him like a flood, and by night a whirlwind carries him away.
notes.limit: The first line of verse 20 names no time; it answers the day only by its place in the crossing. Other writers take lying down in verse 19 as dying, not as going to bed, and do not mark this order.

cites.quote: he lieth down to sleep rich, and he doeth it no more, since in the night he is removed from life ... by sudden death; or also: in the morning he openeth his eyes ... he closes them for ever ... attached crosswise (chiastisch) to this picture of sudden destruction, be it by night or by day: the terrors of death seize him ... like a flood ... by night a whirlwind ... carrieth him away

notes.short: The realm of the dead speaks of wisdom
notes.about: Abaddon and Death, the world of the dead, are made to speak like persons, as the ocean depths do in verse 14. Even there wisdom is known only by a rumor: they have heard of it, but they do not understand it.

figure.name: Personification
figure.means: the world of the dead, which has only heard a distant report of wisdom

original.note: In Hebrew Abaddon means destruction; here, as in Job 26:6, it names the world of the dead.

notes.evidence: Barnes calls the verse a personification, and an exceedingly sublime one; he takes Abaddon, as in Job 26:6, for the world of the dead, whose deep and dark regions had only heard a distant report of wisdom and did not understand it.

cites.quote: Destruction - This is a personification which is exceedingly sublime. ... see the notes at Job 26:6. It is employed here, as in that place, to denote the nether world - the abode of departed spirits ... The sense is, that those deep and dark regions had simply heard the distant report of wisdom but they did not understand it

notes.short: Six troubles, even seven: however many come
notes.about: Eliphaz tells Job that God will rescue him from six calamities, then raises the count to seven. The numbers do not count troubles: they mean that however many come, God is able to deliver from them all.

figure.name: Numerical saying
figure.words: six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven
figure.means: every trouble that may come, however many

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) says six is an indefinite number, one more added to mean every case. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a number, then the next higher, for all possible troubles. Clarke: six and seven are put for many. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): formed like the number proverbs, still more than six. Henry: however often troubles come, God delivers out of them all.
notes.limit: These are Eliphaz's words to Job. The note is on how he counts, not on whether his counsel fit Job's case.

cites.quote: Six is used here to denote an indefinite number, meaning that he would support in many troubles. This mode of speech is not uncommon among the Hebrews, where one number is mentioned, so that an extreme number may be immediately added. The method is, to mention a number within the limit, and then to add one more, meaning that in all instances the thing referred to would occur.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Hebrew idiom fixes on a certain number (here "six"), in order to call attention as to a thing of importance; then increases the force by adding, with a "yea, nay seven," the next higher number; here "seven," the sacred and perfect number. In all possible troubles; not merely in the precise number "seven."

cites.quote: The numbers six and seven are put here for many. Though a number of troubles should come upon thee all at once, and there should be no hope, humanly speaking, yet God would rid thee out of them all
